⚖️💥 Syria: Four Runways, Two Accounts

Israel says it struck Syria’s Abu al-Duhur air base because Damascus was about to allow Turkish troops to deploy there.

The Prime Minister’s Office said Israel and Syria had agreed to a security status quo, and that Syria was about to breach it. 

Israel had repeatedly warned Damascus that a Turkish deployment near Aleppo would threaten Israeli security, the statement said. Israel also said it would welcome a return to the previous arrangement. 

The previous arrangement ended with eight airstrikes on Abu al-Duhur.

Syrian state media said the strikes hit the airfield’s runways. No casualties were reported. Turkey denied that it had personnel at the base and rejected Israel’s explanation as “untenable.” 

Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria, said the attack risked a direct confrontation between Israel and Turkey. Turkish forces, he said, did not know Israeli aircraft were headed toward Abu al-Duhur or why. They could have scrambled fighter jets after concluding that Turkey itself was under attack. 

The United States is now trying to revive a mechanism to prevent Israeli, Turkish and Syrian forces from misreading each other’s movements. It is an effort to restore the communication that was absent before the strike. 

Saudi Arabia called the raid a “flagrant violation” of international law and Syrian sovereignty. Turkey called it an illegal attack. Israel called a possible Turkish deployment a threat to its security. 

Each government has a clear position. Syria has four damaged runways.

🇵🇦 The Panama Canal Authority is tightening draft limits twice in the coming weeks — lowering the maximum vessel draft to 48 feet on August 26, then to 47.5 feet on September 3 — to conserve water in Gatún Lake amid a worsening El Niño-driven drought. Lower draft means ships must carry less cargo per transit, even as the number of daily crossings stays roughly stable.

Major carriers including CMA CGM and Hapag-Lloyd have already introduced transit surcharges, with fees on some routes reaching up to $1,000 per container.
